title: review: LS2b fix round 2: keep the existing event-line format so the jev-exception handover test passes
spec: Fix round of T-1614 (chain T-1612; commit c86caa1 on task/T-1612, also ref task/T-1614). The gate is red on one existing test: tests/test_handover.py::test_handover_survives_jev_exception expects the events tail line 'T-0002 update {"status": "done", "result": {"summary": "ok", "confidence": 0.0, "provenance": ' i.e. `json.dumps(e['data'])[:80]` exactly as before. c86caa1 changed how event data is capped or formatted. Keep the old format for single-line input: the sanitizer only replaces newline-bearing whitespace runs with one space and must leave already single-line text byte-identical; event data keeps its existing [:80] cap (apply the newline collapse to the json text, which json.dumps already makes single-line). Do not weaken the new sanitizer test. A 'RuntimeError: boom' traceback in the log is from a test that raises on purpose. Run tests/test_handover.py and commit.

result.summary: The only change is `_one_line` in orchestrator/handover.py. It now collapses newline-bearing whitespace runs to one space and leaves single-line text byte-identical, which is what the spec asked for. That restores the `json.dumps(...)[:80]` event tail that test_handover_survives_jev_exception expects. The `[:80]` cap is untouched, and the tests file is not modified, so the new sanitizer test is not weakened. I did not run the tests. The diff I reviewed was c86caa1..487a5bf, because the packet showed only a diffstat. One residual gap: other Unicode line separators no longer collapse, though this module never splits on them. All 3 acceptance tests are present.

comments.issue: The regex only treats \r and \n as line breaks. The old `str.split()` approach also collapsed \x0b, \x0c, \x1c-\x1e, \x85, \u2028 and \u2029, which `str.splitlines()` and some Markdown consumers treat as line boundaries. A title or reason containing one of those now passes through intact. handover.py does not use splitlines and the bus text is semi-trusted, so the risk is low. Consider `[\r\n\x0b\x0c\x1c-\x1e\x85\u2028\u2029]` to keep the sanitizer strict while single-line text stays unchanged.
